Will smaller-party performance indirectly hurt the CDU’s chance of finishing first by changing competitive margins between CDU and Greens?
A) No. Smaller-party dynamics do not differentially squeeze CDU versus Greens in a way that costs CDU first place.
B) Yes. Smaller-party performance and threshold effects reshape margins in a way that benefits Greens relative to CDU, denying CDU the most seats.

Is polling error in Baden-Württemberg likely to be small enough that a modest CDU polling lead would usually imply finishing first in seats?
A) Yes. Polling is informative enough here that even a narrow CDU lead would usually translate into finishing first.
B) No. Polling uncertainty, turnout uncertainty, and state-specific error are large enough that a small CDU lead says little about who will actually win most seats.

Will smaller parties’ threshold performance and vote fragmentation translate a CDU vote-share edge into a seat plurality, or conversely deny CDU a seat plurality even if it is close in votes?
A) Yes. The seat-allocation environment will be favorable enough that a narrow CDU lead in votes could plausibly become the largest seat total.
B) No. Seat translation will not especially favor CDU; if CDU is only narrowly competitive in votes, it may still fail to win the most seats.

Does the Baden-Württemberg electoral system make it plausible for a party to win the most seats without winning the most votes, in a way that materially helps or hurts CDU relative to the Greens?
A) Yes. Seat-allocation rules, direct mandates, or threshold effects create a meaningful path for CDU to win the most seats even if the vote margin is narrow.
B) No. Seat totals will track vote shares closely enough that whoever wins votes will almost certainly win seats too.

Will the loss or weakening of Winfried Kretschmann's personal vote advantage materially reduce the Greens' seat share relative to CDU?
A) The loss or weakening of Winfried Kretschmann's personal vote advantage will not materially reduce the Greens' seat share relative to CDU.
B) The loss or weakening of Winfried Kretschmann's personal vote advantage will materially reduce the Greens' seat share relative to CDU.

Is the polling lead, if any, large and consistent enough that sampling error and late campaign movement are unlikely to reverse the party ranking by election day?
A) Yes. The lead is outside ordinary polling noise or is corroborated across multiple pollsters and over time.
B) No. The apparent lead is fragile, within noise, or inconsistent across pollsters, so the ranking is not stable.

Are Baden-Württemberg voting intentions for the next Landtag election likely to track national CDU strength more than state-level incumbent advantages for the Greens?
A) National partisan trends are likely to dominate, so CDU strength at the federal level will translate strongly into the Baden-Württemberg election.
B) State-level incumbent advantages for the Greens are likely to outweigh national CDU strength, making Baden-Württemberg more exceptional than national trends imply.

Are late-cycle Baden-Württemberg polls likely to show the CDU ahead of the Greens in vote share?
A) Most credible late polls will show the CDU narrowly or clearly ahead of the Greens in vote share.
B) Most credible late polls will show the Greens tied with or ahead of the CDU in vote share.

Is the federal political environment by election time likely to favor CDU in Baden-Württemberg rather than generating backlash that helps the Greens?
A) Yes. National conditions at election time are likely to strengthen CDU’s brand in the state more than they strengthen the Greens'.
B) No. National conditions by election time are as likely to hurt CDU or help the Greens as the reverse.

At the time of the election, will state-level voting intention polls show the CDU clearly ahead of the Greens rather than in a tie or behind?
A) Yes. Polls near election day will show the CDU with a real and stable lead over the Greens.
B) No. Polls will show either a toss-up or a Greens lead, implying the CDU is not structurally ahead.

Will vote fragmentation among SPD, FDP, AfD, and smaller parties convert a modest CDU vote advantage into the most seats, rather than leaving seat leadership dependent mainly on whether Greens or CDU actually finish first in votes?
A) Seat allocation and threshold effects will likely help a modest CDU edge translate into the largest seat total.
B) Seat allocation will not materially rescue the CDU; winning the most seats will mostly require actually beating the Greens in vote share.

Is there enough time before the election for major opinion shifts that could plausibly overturn the current ranking between CDU and Greens?
A) No. There is not much time, so current standings are relatively sticky.
B) Yes. There is ample time for substantial movement before election day.

Are smaller parties likely to win enough votes and seats to alter which of CDU or Greens ends up with the largest seat total?
A) Smaller parties' performance will not materially distort the CDU's path to winning the most seats; the seat outcome will mostly track the CDU-Greens vote gap.
B) Smaller parties will matter enough that even a close CDU vote result may not translate into the most seats, or they will help preserve a Greens lead in seats.

Do national political trends by election time favor CDU enough to outweigh Baden-Württemberg’s state-specific pattern?
A) No. National trends either do not favor CDU enough, or are offset by state-specific conditions, so CDU does not gain enough from federal momentum.
B) Yes. National political conditions swing sufficiently toward CDU that they dominate state-specific countervailing factors and lift CDU into first place.

Are late-campaign polls and public indicators systematically understating CDU relative to the Greens in this election?
A) No. Polls are broadly accurate or even slightly flatter the CDU; there is no hidden CDU reservoir large enough to put them first.
B) Yes. Polling misses a late CDU shift, shy/undecided CDU-leaning voters, or turnout composition that leaves CDU stronger than headline polls suggest.

Do Baden-Württemberg-specific political dynamics outweigh national party trends in determining which party wins the most seats?
A) No. State-specific dynamics are not strong enough to fully offset broader partisan trends this time.
B) Yes. Baden-Württemberg's distinctive state politics dominate enough that national swings matter less than usual.

Will pre-election Baden-Württemberg polling close to election day show CDU ahead of the Greens by enough that ordinary polling error is unlikely to erase the lead?
A) Pre-election polling close to election day will show CDU ahead of the Greens by a margin large enough that typical polling error is unlikely to overturn it.
B) Pre-election polling close to election day will show only a narrow CDU-Green gap, or no reliable CDU lead, such that ordinary polling error could easily change the ranking.

Is the CDU better positioned than the Greens to consolidate support from ideologically adjacent voters?
A) The CDU will consolidate the center-right vote more effectively than the Greens consolidate the center-left/ecologist vote.
B) The Greens will consolidate their broader anti-CDU and incumbent-friendly electorate at least as effectively as the CDU consolidates the right.

Is Baden-Württemberg's recent pattern of Green outperformance unusually vulnerable to national-level backlash against the Greens by the time of the election?
A) Yes. Federal dissatisfaction with Green policies will spill over strongly into the Land election and disproportionately depress Green support.
B) No. Baden-Württemberg voters distinguish state from federal politics, and any national Green weakness will only partially transmit to the Land election.

Is national political mood by election time likely to favor CDU enough to spill over materially into the Baden-Württemberg state election?
A) Yes. The broader environment will tilt toward CDU, and voters will use the state election partly to reward or align with a stronger CDU brand nationally.
B) No. State-specific factors will dominate, so any national CDU strength will have limited effect on who finishes first in Baden-Württemberg.

Are smaller-party dynamics and coalition-related tactical voting more likely to help the Greens than the CDU in the race for first place?
A) Tactical voting and smaller-party voter flows do not meaningfully boost the Greens’ top-line result and may even fragment the center-left/green camp.
B) Tactical voting and smaller-party voter flows disproportionately help the Greens remain the largest party, especially among voters prioritizing blocking the CDU or preserving a Green-led government.

Will the leading state-level candidates and campaign in Baden-Württemberg favor CDU more than Greens by election day?
A) The leading state-level candidates and campaign in Baden-Württemberg will not favor CDU more than Greens by election day.
B) The leading state-level candidates and campaign in Baden-Württemberg will favor CDU more than Greens by election day.

Will the Greens still lead or be effectively tied for first in Baden-Württemberg vote intention polling close to the election campaign?
A) Yes. The Greens will still be polling first or essentially tied near the election, making CDU seat plurality an underdog outcome.
B) No. The Greens will not hold a lead near the campaign; CDU will be clearly ahead or at least more likely to finish first in votes.

Will Winfried Kretschmann's personal or legacy effect continue to materially boost Green vote share relative to a generic Green baseline?
A) Yes. Kretschmann's personal popularity or political legacy will still provide the Greens with a meaningful boost, helping them stay ahead of or level with CDU.
B) No. Any Kretschmann effect will fade substantially, and without a strong personal boost the Greens will not gain much extra support beyond their generic party level.

By the time of the election, will Baden-Württemberg still behave as a state where the Greens have an unusual structural advantage relative to their national baseline?
A) No. The state will revert toward a more conventional center-right pattern, with the Greens losing some of their exceptional Baden-Württemberg advantage.
B) Yes. Baden-Württemberg remains a special stronghold for the Greens, and that structural advantage persists beyond one election cycle.
